articles.headline: OFAC Designates Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations for Narcotics and Terrorism
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated three Guatemalan drug trafficking organizations (DTOs) – Los Lorenzana, Los Mendoza, and Los Huistas – for their involvement in narcotics trafficking and support for Mexican narco-terrorist cartels. These designations were made under counter-narcotics and counter-terrorism authorities, including Executive Order 13224, as amended by Executive Order 13886, and Executive Order 14059.

Los Lorenzana, also known as the Lorenzana Drug Trafficking Organization, 'The Lorenzana Clan,' and 'The Lorenzana Family,' has been identified as a transnational terrorist group and criminal organization. The Los Mendoza DTO, operating across Guatemala, Honduras, and Belize, and the Los Huistas DTO, based in various locations within Guatemala, were also designated as criminal organizations.

These actions aim to disrupt the financial and logistical support provided by these Guatemalan networks to major Mexican cartels, including the Sinaloa Cartel and Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación. The designations carry secondary sanctions risks, further isolating these groups from the international financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Sanctions List, Amends Alias for Volta Shipping Services
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an update to its Iran sanctions program, specifically amending the alias for Volta Shipping Services LLC. The UAE-based company, linked to Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani, will now be listed with the alias Volta Container Line FZCO, in addition to its previous alias Volta Shipping Services FZCO.

Volta Shipping Services LLC remains designated under Executive Order 13902, which targets the digital asset sector of the Iranian economy. This update signifies OFAC's ongoing efforts to refine and maintain the accuracy of its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

The company continues to be subject to secondary sanctions risk, highlighting the potential consequences for foreign financial institutions that knowingly facilitate significant transactions for designated Iranian entities.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Eight Canada-Based Money Services Businesses for Iran-Related Digital Asset Activities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has sanctioned eight Canada-based money services businesses (MSBs) for their alleged involvement in operating within the digital asset sector of the Iranian economy. This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targets international financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions.

According to OFAC, these businesses facilitate transactions involving Iran, including converting Iranian currency into digital assets and conducting transactions with sanctioned Iranian exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Several of the designated entities are also alleged to have sent or received funds from addresses associated with terrorism and to have laundered drug proceeds.

The designations were made under Executive Order 13902 and were coordinated with FinCEN, Canada's financial intelligence unit (FINTRAC), and the Drug Enforcement Administration. This action follows previous rounds of Iran-related sanctions targeting digital asset exchanges in Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Global Scam Networks, Cuban Regime, and Designates Vessels
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a series of designations targeting global scam networks, the corporate infrastructure enabling them, and entities linked to the Cuban regime. This action includes the publication of a Cuba-related Determination pursuant to Executive Order 14404, specifically addressing the 'Electronics, Manufacturing, Marine, and Technology Sectors of the Cuban Economy.'

Among the new additions to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List are entities involved in gambling and betting activities, such as ASIAN WELFARE LOTTERIES CO LTD in Cambodia, and BEIJING H AND C TECHNOLOGIES CO., LTD in China, linked to transnational criminal organizations. OFAC also designated several vessels, including the LPG Tanker EMILIA and the Chemical/Products Tanker GLORIA C, both flagged in Cuba and linked to Cuban state-owned enterprises.

These designations were made under authorities related to cyber-related activities, transnational criminal organizations, and Cuba sanctions. The action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to countering cybercrime, fraud, and predatory schemes targeting Americans, as outlined in Executive Order 14390.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, alongside updates to certain existing Iran-related listings. Concurrently, OFAC published an Iran-related alert and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question.

Significantly, OFAC added a 'Secondary sanctions risk' warning to over 1,000 existing entries on the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, primarily those designated under Executive Order 13902, and to the Sectoral Sanctions Identifications (SSI) List entry for VTB Bank. This change serves as a clear warning to foreign banks regarding the potential loss of U.S. correspondent and payable-through accounts if they knowingly facilitate significant transactions for blocked persons.

While no new entities were designated through this specific update, the enhanced visibility of secondary sanctions risk on the SDN list is expected to lead to faster payment rejections and increased de-risking of Iran-linked business by financial institutions. The Iran-related alert also warns against the use of false flags by the Iranian 'shadow fleet' to evade sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License for Wind Down of Transactions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Iran General License FF-1, titled 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.' This amended general license provides authorization for activities ordinarily incident and necessary to wind down transactions with the specified entity.

This action is part of OFAC's ongoing management of its sanctions programs, allowing for an orderly cessation of certain financial dealings while maintaining the broader sanctions regime against Iran. The issuance of wind-down licenses is a common practice when OFAC seeks to adjust the scope of its prohibitions or to facilitate the exit of parties from previously authorized activities.

Entities engaged in transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance should carefully review the terms and deadlines outlined in General License FF-1 to ensure compliance and avoid potential sanctions violations.

articles.region: North Korea / Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities for North Korea and DRC-Related Activities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in activities related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to disrupt networks facilitating illicit activities and supporting destabilizing actors in both regions.

Under the North Korea sanctions program, OFAC added several individuals, including Russian and North Korean nationals, and entities such as FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER, which operates in financial and insurance activities in North Korea and Russia. These designations target facilitators of DPRK IT worker fraud, which often targets U.S. businesses.

For the Democratic Republic of the Congo, designations include entities linked to the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and a Kigali-based financial institution, Zigama Credit and Savings Society (Zigama CSS), for their alleged support of the M23 rebel group. These actions underscore the U.S. commitment to addressing human rights abuses and regional instability.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations. Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and related services to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer.

MMZA was majority-owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey, a designated entity since July 2014, making MMZA a blocked person by operation of law, even though MMZA itself was not directly listed on the SDN List until June 2022. OFAC determined that Extreme Networks failed to conduct sufficient due diligence to identify MMZA as a blocked entity, despite red flags and the company's U.S.-led compliance team reviewing the purchase agreements.

The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination that the violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. This case highlights the importance of comprehensive sanctions compliance programs that extend beyond name-only screening and include thorough due diligence on ownership structures, especially in high-risk jurisdictions.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Extreme Networks, Inc.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Frequently Asked Questions on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has amended several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update is part of OFAC's ongoing process to review and ensure its published guidance remains current.

The revised FAQs, including numbers 10, 32 through 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53, provide clarifications on various aspects of sanctions compliance. Key areas addressed include distinguishing between blocking and rejecting transactions, the requirements for interest on blocked funds, permissible deductions of service charges, customer notification procedures, and the timing and format for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions.

While these amendments do not introduce new sanctions programs or designations, they offer crucial guidance for financial institutions and other U.S. persons to ensure proper handling of sanctions-related matters and accurate reporting to OFAC. Compliance teams should review these updated FAQs to align their internal procedures with OFAC's latest guidance.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Amends FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. Additionally, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs).

This action reflects OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, adjusting its lists and guidance in response to evolving geopolitical landscapes and compliance needs. The issuance of new general licenses provides specific authorizations for certain transactions, while the amended FAQs aim to clarify existing regulations and reporting requirements for various sanctions programs.

Entities operating in or with connections to Iran, Belarus, North Korea, or Russia should carefully review these updates to ensure ongoing compliance with OFAC's regulations, particularly regarding the new designations, removals, and the scope of the general licenses.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Fined $1,529,685 by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations. The violations involved nine instances of exporting networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer, Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), between September 2018 and March 2022.

MMZA was deemed a blocked person due to its majority ownership by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey, an entity designated by OFAC in 2014, even though MMZA itself was not directly listed until 2022. OFAC determined that Extreme Networks failed to conduct adequate due diligence to identify MMZA as a blocked entity, despite its compliance team reviewing relevant contracts.

The settlement amount reflects that the violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and considered egregious. This case underscores the critical importance of comprehensive sanctions screening and due diligence, particularly when dealing with entities in high-risk jurisdictions or those with complex ownership structures.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle apparent violations of various sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism. This settlement was part of a coordinated enforcement action that also involved the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).

The violations stemmed from the bank's failure to implement and maintain an adequate anti-money laundering (AML) program and to conduct proper due diligence on foreign financial institution correspondent accounts. These deficiencies led to the late reporting of over $5 billion in suspicious activity.

The OFAC settlement highlights the severe consequences for financial institutions that fail to adhere to sanctions compliance obligations. The bank admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and FinCEN's implementing regulations.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors, Transfers to EAR
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR). This deregulatory action transfers control from the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This change aligns export controls on suppressors with the controls already applied to firearms, aiming to streamline the regulatory process. The move is part of an ongoing effort to rationalize export control categories and reduce administrative burdens where appropriate.

Exporters of these items should familiarize themselves with the updated regulations under the EAR to ensure compliance with the new requirements. The change is expected to simplify the export process for legitimate trade while maintaining national security considerations.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
